details.heading: What AI adds to automation
paragraphs: Traditional automation moves information along fixed paths. AI models add the ability to read and interpret: understanding what an email is asking, pulling details out of a document, summarising a long thread or drafting a reply in your tone. Combined, they can handle processes that used to need a person at every step.

details.heading: Which work is worth automating
paragraphs: The best candidates are tasks your team does often, the same way each time, and that mostly move information from one place to another. If a task needs real judgement on every case, it may suit an AI agent with a person approving, or it may be better left as it is.
points: It happens every day or every week
It follows roughly the same steps each time
It means copying details between tools, inboxes or spreadsheets
Delays cost you something: a slow reply, a missed follow-up, a late report

details.heading: Benefits and limitations
paragraphs: Done well, automation reduces time spent on routine tasks, makes responses more consistent and keeps information up to date across your tools. How much it helps depends on how often a task happens and how much of it follows a pattern, so we estimate it from your process rather than promising a figure.

AI has limits too. Language models can misread an unusual request or state something incorrect with confidence. That is why we test on real cases, ground answers in your own information, and keep a person approving anything that commits your business.
points: Good fit: frequent, repetitive tasks with clear inputs
Good fit: work that is mostly reading, sorting or moving information
Poor fit: decisions that need expert judgement on every case
Poor fit: processes that change completely from one week to the next

paragraphs: Typical applications, described as possibilities rather than past client results:
points: A website enquiry is categorised, logged in your CRM and a draft reply is prepared for your approval

details.heading: Human oversight: people stay in control
paragraphs: An automation should make your team faster, not hide what is happening. We decide with you which steps run on their own and which wait for a person to approve, and we keep a record of what each workflow did.
Before anything goes live, we test it on real past cases. If a step fails, the workflow stops and tells someone, rather than carrying on with bad information.

details.heading: Working with the tools you already use
paragraphs: We connect the CRM, inbox, forms and spreadsheets you already have, wherever they offer a supported connection, instead of asking you to switch. Where a workflow uses a paid third-party tool or an AI service, we tell you the running cost before we build it.

details.heading: How we implement it
paragraphs: We start small: one workflow, mapped with the people who do the work today. Once the design is agreed in writing, we build it, test it on real past cases and, where it makes sense, run it alongside the manual process for a short period before switching over. You get documentation, and after launch we review how it performs and adjust.

faq.q: What kind of business is AI automation suitable for?
faq.a: Any business where the same manual steps repeat every day: answering similar enquiries, chasing leads, copying details between tools or preparing the same report each week. Small teams often feel the benefit most, because those hours come out of a few people’s days.

faq.q: Do we need technical knowledge to use it?
faq.a: No. We build and connect the workflow, test it with you and hand over plain notes on how it works. Your team keeps using the tools they already know.

faq.q: Will automation replace our staff?
faq.a: That isn’t the aim. Automation takes on the repetitive steps so your team can spend more time on customers and on work that needs judgement.

faq.q: What happens if an automation makes a mistake?
faq.a: Steps that matter wait for a person to approve them, every run is logged, and a failed step stops the workflow and alerts someone. We also test on real past cases before going live.

faq.q: How is this different from AI agent development?
faq.a: Automation follows the steps you define, with AI helping on parts such as reading or drafting. An AI agent decides how to handle each case within limits you set. Many projects start with automation; we suggest an agent only when the work needs it.

faq.q: How is AI automation different from workflow automation?
faq.a: Our Workflow Automation service connects tools and automates rule-based steps. AI Automation adds AI models for the steps that involve reading, interpreting or drafting text. Many projects combine both.

faq.q: How long does it take to automate a workflow?
faq.a: It depends on the number of steps and tools involved. One well-defined workflow is a much smaller project than a process that spans several systems. We give you a timeline in the written scope once we have mapped the work.

details.heading: What an AI agent is
paragraphs: An AI agent is software that uses a language model to work through a task: it reads what has come in, decides what kind of case it is, and takes the next step using the tools it has been given, such as looking up a record, drafting a reply or updating your CRM.
Unlike a chatbot, an agent doesn’t just answer questions. It does a piece of work, and it can be set up to stop and ask a person whenever it reaches a decision it shouldn’t make alone.

details.heading: Automation or an agent: which do you need?
paragraphs: If the steps are the same every time, a workflow automation is simpler, cheaper and more predictable. An agent earns its place when each case is a little different and needs reading and judgement before anything happens.
points: Automation: the same input leads to the same steps, every time
Agent: the input varies, and the right next step depends on what it says
Often the answer is both: an automation hands the unclear cases to an agent, and the agent hands the hard ones to a person

details.heading: Business applications
paragraphs: Good first projects are tasks with plenty of volume, a clear definition of a good result and a person who can review the output.
points: Reading and sorting incoming enquiries and support requests
Drafting replies and quotes from your own information for approval
Checking documents or forms against a list of requirements
Keeping CRM records and spreadsheets up to date
Preparing research summaries and briefings for your team

details.heading: Tool integration
paragraphs: An agent is only as useful as the tools it can use. We connect agents to your systems through their APIs or supported integrations, such as your CRM, helpdesk, inbox, calendar, spreadsheets or document store, and give each one a defined set of actions: look up a record, draft a reply, create a task, update a field.

details.heading: Approval controls
paragraphs: You decide which actions an agent may take on its own and which need a person’s sign-off. Typical rules: anything sent to a customer, any price or commitment, and any change to financial or personal records waits for approval. The agent prepares the work; a person confirms it.

details.heading: Security considerations
paragraphs: An agent gets only the access its job needs, with its own credentials where the tool allows. Before anything is connected, we explain which AI provider processes your data and under what terms, avoid sending data the task doesn’t need, and keep a log of every action the agent takes.

details.heading: Monitoring and maintenance
paragraphs: After launch, we review the agent’s logs and outputs with you, look at the cases it handed to a person, and refine its instructions, information and limits. AI models and the tools they connect to change over time, so agents need periodic checks to keep working as intended.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent?
faq.a: A chatbot answers questions in a conversation. An AI agent carries out a task, such as sorting an enquiry, updating a record or preparing a reply, using the tools it has been connected to.

faq.q: Can an agent work with our existing software?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Agents connect to tools that offer an API or a supported integration, such as many CRMs, inboxes, forms and spreadsheets. We check your tools before we propose anything.

faq.q: Can we control what the agent is allowed to do?
faq.a: Yes. You decide its limits, which actions need a person’s approval and what it must always hand over. Those rules are part of the written scope.

faq.q: Is our business data safe?
faq.a: The agent gets only the access it needs, and we tell you which AI provider processes your data and under what terms before anything is connected. Sensitive actions can always require approval.

faq.q: Do we need an AI agent or a simpler automation?
faq.a: If the steps are the same every time, a simpler automation is usually the better choice. We’ll tell you which fits after looking at the work itself.

faq.q: What happens if the agent gets something wrong?
faq.a: Because sensitive actions wait for approval, most mistakes are caught before they reach a customer. Every action is logged, so an error can be traced and the agent’s instructions or limits adjusted. We test on real past cases before launch to find weak spots early.

workflow-automation.title: Workflow Automation
workflow-automation.heading: Connect Your Tools. {Automate Repetitive Processes.}
workflow-automation.summary: We map your business processes, connect the tools involved and automate the repetitive, rule-based steps, with error handling and monitoring so you can rely on the result.
workflow-automation.who: Businesses where the same information is re-typed between forms, inboxes, CRMs, spreadsheets and accounting tools, or where tasks wait for someone to pass them on.
workflow-automation.problem: Most businesses run on several tools that don’t talk to each other. People bridge the gaps by copying, pasting and reminding each other, and details get missed or entered twice.
includes: Mapping the current process step by step, with the people who run it
Designing the automated flow, its triggers and its exceptions
Connecting the tools involved and building the workflow
Adding error handling, alerts and logging
Testing, launch, documentation and monitoring

principles.title: Failures are visible
principles.text: If a step fails, the workflow stops and alerts someone, instead of passing on bad data.

details.heading: How this differs from AI automation
paragraphs: Workflow automation handles processes with clear rules: when this happens, do that. It doesn’t need AI to work, which makes it predictable and inexpensive to run. When a step involves reading or interpreting text, such as understanding an email or drafting a reply, we add AI to the workflow. That is what our AI Automation service covers.

details.heading: Workflow mapping comes first
paragraphs: Before building anything, we document how the process runs today with the people who do it. This often reveals steps that can be removed entirely, which is cheaper than automating them.
points: What starts the process
Every step, tool and hand-off

details.heading: Error handling and monitoring
paragraphs: Real-world data is messy: a form is missing a field, a service is briefly unavailable, a record already exists. We design for these cases with validation, retries and alerts to a named person when something needs attention. Every run is logged, so you can see what happened and when.

details.heading: Integrations with the tools you use
paragraphs: We connect tools through their official APIs and integrations, and check that your software supports what the workflow needs before proposing anything. Where a workflow relies on a paid platform, we tell you the running cost up front.

faq.q: What is workflow automation?
faq.a: Software that carries out the steps of a business process automatically when something happens, such as a form submission, a new email or a scheduled time. It moves information between tools, creates records, sends notifications and triggers the next step.

faq.q: Which tools can you connect?
faq.a: Most modern business software with an API or built-in integrations can be connected, including many CRMs, email providers, form builders, spreadsheets, calendars and accounting tools. We confirm what’s possible with your specific tools before proposing a solution.

faq.q: Do we need AI for workflow automation?
faq.a: No. Many valuable workflows are purely rule-based. We add AI only where a step needs reading, classifying or drafting text.

faq.q: What happens if a workflow fails?
faq.a: It stops, logs the error and alerts the person responsible, rather than carrying on with incomplete data. We design and test these failure cases before launch.

faq.q: Can you improve workflows we already have?
faq.a: Yes. We can review existing automations, fix fragile steps, add error handling and monitoring, or rebuild them where that is simpler.

details.heading: What an AI readiness assessment covers
paragraphs: We look at your key workflows, the tools and data they depend on, and how your team works today. The result is a short written report that names the most promising opportunities, the risks and prerequisites of each, and a recommended order.

details.heading: Risk and responsible use
paragraphs: AI brings specific risks: incorrect outputs, data sent to third-party providers, dependence on a single vendor, and decisions made without enough oversight. We assess these for each opportunity and recommend controls, such as approval steps, access limits and logging, before anything is built.

details.heading: From roadmap to implementation and ongoing improvement
paragraphs: A roadmap is only useful if it gets done. You can take it to your own team or another provider, or ask us to implement the parts we build: workflow automation, AI automation and custom AI agents. Once solutions are running, we can review them periodically and refine them as your processes and the available tools change.

faq.q: What does an AI consulting engagement involve?
faq.a: A conversation about your goals, a review of the workflows and tools involved, and a written, prioritised roadmap. The scope and price are agreed in writing before we start.

faq.q: Do we need data or technical staff in place first?
faq.a: No. Part of the assessment is understanding what you already have and what each opportunity would need. Many useful automations work with the tools and records a business already keeps.

faq.q: Will you only recommend your own services?
faq.a: No. If the best option is an off-the-shelf tool, a process change or another provider, the roadmap says so.

faq.q: How do you handle data privacy?
faq.a: We identify what data each opportunity involves, which providers would process it and under what terms, and recommend controls before anything is connected. We avoid sending data a task doesn’t need.

faq.q: Can you help put the roadmap into action?
faq.a: Yes, for the parts we build: workflow automation, AI automation and custom AI agents. For anything else, the roadmap explains what to look for.

faq.q: Do you build custom websites, or use WordPress and Shopify?
faq.a: Both. A custom build suits sites with specific needs or a web application. WordPress or Shopify suits businesses that want to update pages or products themselves. We recommend one at the start and explain why.

faq.q: Will the website work properly on phones?
faq.a: Yes. Most visitors arrive on a phone, so we design for that screen first and test on phones, tablets and desktops before launch.

faq.q: Can we update the website ourselves after launch?
faq.a: Yes. We hand over the logins and notes you need, and choose a platform your team can manage.

faq.q: Do you redesign existing websites?
faq.a: Yes. We review what the current site does well and where visitors drop off, then make the changes that make it clearer, faster and easier to use.

faq.q: Do you also handle SEO or digital marketing?
faq.a: We build sites with search engines in mind: clear page titles and descriptions, fast pages, a sitemap and a clean structure. We don’t currently run ongoing SEO or advertising campaigns.

details.heading: Built to turn visitors into enquiries
paragraphs: A business website has one main job: help the right visitors understand what you offer and make it easy for them to get in touch. We plan each page around the questions visitors arrive with, place clear calls to action where they are needed and keep forms short.

details.heading: Technical SEO foundations
paragraphs: Every site we build includes the technical groundwork search engines expect: a logical heading structure, unique page titles and descriptions, clean URLs, canonical tags, an XML sitemap, structured data where it applies, and compressed images. We don’t currently run ongoing SEO or advertising campaigns, but the site is ready for them.

details.heading: Performance and responsive design
paragraphs: Most visitors arrive on a phone, often on a mobile connection. We design for small screens first, keep pages light, load images and video only when needed, and test on real devices and browsers before launch.

details.heading: Integrations
paragraphs: A website can connect to the tools you already use: enquiry forms that reach your inbox or CRM, booking calendars, WhatsApp, analytics and e-commerce platforms. Where it helps, a website can also feed an automation, for example routing each new enquiry to the right person.
